newsitem.title: USA: PG&E sets $14 mln Diablo Canyon settlement.
newsitem.headline: PG&E sets $14 mln Diablo Canyon settlement.

text.p: PG&E Corp's Pacific Gas and Electric Co. will pay more than $14 million to settle allegations it violated clean water laws at its Diablo Canyon nuclear power plant, U.S. and state officials said Tuesday.
A consent decree settling one of the largest environmental cases in California history was filed Tuesday in U.S. District Court in San Francisco, they said.

California and federal agencies alleged that PG&E violated state and federal clean water laws at the Diablo Canyon plant by submitting incomplete and misleading data on the amount of sea life drawn into its water cooling system.
The 2,200-megawatt Diablo Canyon plant is near San Luis Obispo on the central California coast.

"State and federal environmental officials must be able to rely on the accuracy of the information submitted under our environmental laws so they can protect public health and the environment," Lois Schiffer, assistant U.S. attorney general in charge of the Justice Department's Environment and Natural Resources Division, said in a statement.
"The message here is clear: if you mislead agencies responsible for protecting our environment, you will pay a heavy price," Schiffer said.

The U.S. and California environmental protection agencies alleged in lawsuits that PG&E omitted sampling data on the amount of sea life, such as small fish and other organisms, killed by the 2.5 billion gallon per day cooling water intake system at Diablo Canyon, the Justice Department said.
The agencies alleged that PG&E omitted more than half of the actual test results which showed up to a 90 percent reduction in sea life as it passed through the cooling system.

The measurements and reports are required by permits issued under state and federal clean water laws to ensure that companies use the best technology available to lessen environmental harm caused by their operations.
More than $6 million of the settlement will be used to fund two environmental projects, the Justice Department said.

It said $3.7 million would go to estuary protection measures in the Morro Bay area of the California coast and $2.5 million for the state's mussel watch program which studies mussels to monitor water quality.
PG&E is carrying out a new study of the impact of its cooling water intake system on sea life, state officials said.

"We're pleased to be able to bring this to a conclusion and move forward and produce some new studies that we think will confirm that there is no and has been no environmental impact," Jeff Lewis, PG&E's Diablo Canyon spokesman, said.
He said the company denied deliberately withholding information.
The Diablo Canyon nuclear power plant provides power to about two million Californians.
